what: Build Check Part 3 (the plain read, ROC Operations Manual §14.2A): a session that saw only Pip's statements read them as a gardener would, sentence by sentence. First read of version 0.1, second read of version 0.2.

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In most of Australia, the main winter pruning is done in July. In some places it can start in June. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In a cold or frosty area, wait until August to prune, so that frost does not damage the new shoots. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In New South Wales, near the coast where frosts are rare or never come, July is the time to prune. One rose society says you can start in late June. Inland, or where frosts are regular, it says to prune in August. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in New South Wales only

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In Victoria, one rose society says the best time to prune is June or July. In a cold area, it says to wait until August, so that frost does not knock back the new shoots. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In South Australia, prune in July. One nursery says pruning can start in late June. In a frost area, one rose society says to wait until August; the nursery says July. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In Western Australia, one rose society says to prune in winter, in June and July. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: In Brisbane, one public rose garden says the best time to prune is June or July. One rose farm there prunes in July. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near Brisbane only

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: I couldn't find months for rose jobs written for Tasmania. A local rose society is the place to ask.

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: I couldn't find months for rose jobs written for the Northern Territory. A local garden society or botanic garden is the place to ask.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in the Northern Territory only

statements.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements.text: I couldn't find months for rose jobs written for the dry inland of Australia, such as Alice Springs or Mildura. A local rose society is the place to ask.

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: Start feeding in spring, after the winter prune, as new growth appears. One nursery waits until the rose has plenty of leaves and its first blooms.

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: Give the first feed of spring in the second half of August or in September. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: Give the last feed in late summer or early autumn, in February or March. Two rose societies feed later, into April or May, and one nursery says not to feed in late autumn. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: In New South Wales, one rose society gives the first feed after the winter prune and says the second half of August is ideal, or September in a cold area. It gives the last feed in mid to late February. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in New South Wales only

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: In Victoria, one rose society says to feed roses at the end of August. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: In Victoria, one rose society says not to feed a newly planted bare-root rose (a dormant plant sold in winter, with no leaves or flowers) until late November or early December. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: In South Australia, feed in September and again in February. One rose society says early in September, and in March if you missed February. On sandy soil it feeds four times: in September, November, February and April. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements.text: In Western Australia, one rose society says to feed as new growth appears in early spring, in August or September, and to keep feeding into May. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: I couldn't find a month to stop deadheading (cutting off the finished blooms) in Australia. A local rose society is the place to ask.

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: For more flowers in autumn, give the rose a light trim in summer or early autumn. This is done between January and April, depending on where you live. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: In New South Wales, one rose society says to trim roses in summer for flowers in autumn: in January in a cool area, early in February in a mild area, and in March in a warm area. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in New South Wales only

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: In Victoria, one rose society says to give a summer trim in February if you are timing the flowers for a show or special event. It is still deadheading in April. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: In South Australia, a light trim in late summer or early autumn brings on the autumn flowers. One nursery says mid February, and one rose society says one to two weeks after the February feed. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements.text: In Western Australia, one rose society says to give a light summer prune, taking off about one-third, in March or April, and to keep deadheading into May. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: In Australia, plant a bare-root rose (a dormant plant sold in winter, with no leaves or flowers) in June or July. Planting can start in May. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: Move an established rose in winter, while it is dormant.

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: Don't plant a rose in very hot weather.

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: In New South Wales, one rose society says to prepare the soil in late April or May, for planting in June or July. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in New South Wales only

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: In Sydney, one garden centre says a rose in a pot can be planted at any time of year, though not in very hot weather.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in or near Sydney only

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: In Victoria, one rose society says to order new roses in May and start planting them in June. June is also its month for moving an established rose. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: In South Australia, plant a bare-root rose in June or July. One rose society says planting can go on until early August, and one nursery says bare-root roses can still be planted in August. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements.text: In Western Australia, one rose society says to plant new roses in May, and to plant or repot as needed in June and July. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: After the winter prune, pick off any leaves left on the rose, clear up the prunings and fallen leaves, and get rid of them. One source says to put them in the rubbish bin, not the compost.

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: If you use a clean-up spray in winter (a spray to clear pests and diseases left on the plant), put it on after pruning. Lime sulphur, copper and oil are the types used. Follow the label on the spray.

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: If you use lime sulphur as a winter spray, put it on while the rose is dormant, before new growth appears. One source says lime sulphur burns new growth. Follow the label on the spray.

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In New South Wales, one rose society says to put the prunings and fallen leaves in the green waste bin as soon as pruning is finished, in July, and then to spray with a fungicide or lime sulphur. Follow the label on the spray. Months are only a guide.
statements.shown_to: Gardeners in New South Wales only

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In Victoria, one rose society says to take all the leaves off the bushes and rake up around the beds in July. It then sprays the bare roses, and lightly the ground around them, with copper and white oil, or with lime sulphur. Follow the label on the spray. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In South Australia, clear up the prunings and fallen leaves after pruning, and then spray. One nursery does this in July and one rose society in August. Oil, lime sulphur and copper are the sprays used. Follow the label on the spray. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: In Western Australia, one rose society says to spray after pruning, in June or July, to clean up pests and disease. Follow the label on the spray. Months are only a guide.

statements.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements.text: I couldn't find Australian advice on covering roses or mounding soil over the base for winter. A local rose society is the place to ask.

statements.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements.text: When to do each rose job depends on where you live. Conditions vary across Australia and from one part of a state to another, and one source says even between neighbouring suburbs.

statements.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements.text: In an area that gets frosts, wait until the last frost has passed before you prune.

statements.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements.text: Large areas of northern Australia are generally free of frost, the national weather bureau says. Days cold enough for frost fall mainly between late autumn and early spring.

statements.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements.text: Frost is local: how severe it is can vary a lot over a very small area, the national weather bureau says. Valleys often get frost when the land around them stays free of it.

statements.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements.text: In a humid climate, roses are more likely to get fungal diseases, and one source says they are harder to manage in the hot tropics. Another says to choose a rose that is not prone to these diseases if your climate is humid.

statements.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements.text: In South Australia, one rose society says it is colder and wetter in the Adelaide Hills, the South-East, and Southern Yorke Peninsula and Eyre Peninsula, and that frosts are common in country areas.

statements.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements.text: In Queensland, one rose society says growing and climate conditions vary across the state, so try things and see what works for you.

flags.sentence: In some places it can start in June.
flags.problem: 3: 'some places' is too vague to act on
flags.suggestion: Say it can start in June in milder areas, or remove.

flags.sentence: It is still deadheading in April.
flags.problem: 3: unclear what it means; reads as a fragment
flags.suggestion: Reword as: 'It says you are still deadheading in April.'

flags.sentence: Don't plant a rose in very hot weather.
flags.problem: 3: no months or temperature given, too vague to act on
flags.suggestion: Reword as: 'Plant in winter, not in a hot spell.' or remove.

flags.sentence: Oil, lime sulphur and copper are the sprays used.
flags.problem: 6: repeats the national statement listing lime sulphur, copper and oil

flags.sentence: When to do each rose job depends on where you live.
flags.problem: 2: states the obvious; repeats every 'Months are only a guide' line
flags.suggestion: Remove, or start with 'Frost and climate vary even between neighbouring suburbs, so watch your own garden.'

flags.sentence: In an area that gets frosts, wait until the last frost has passed before you prune.
flags.problem: 6: could confuse with the pruning answer, which says July or August, not 'after the last frost'
flags.suggestion: Reword as: 'In a frosty area, prune later, and wait until frosts have eased.'

flags.sentence: Large areas of northern Australia are generally free of frost, the national weather bureau says.
flags.problem: 1: about the source and a weather report; nothing to do
flags.suggestion: Reword: 'In northern Australia frost is rare, so frost timing matters less there.'

flags.sentence: Frost is local: how severe it is can vary a lot over a very small area, the national weather bureau says.
flags.problem: 1: attributes to the source rather than telling the gardener what to do
flags.suggestion: Reword: 'Frost varies a lot over a small area, and valleys often get frost when the land around them stays free of it. Check your own garden.'

flags.sentence: In South Australia, one rose society says it is colder and wetter in the Adelaide Hills...
flags.problem: 3: describes places but gives no action
flags.suggestion: Reword to say what to do, e.g. 'In these areas, expect later pruning and feeding than on the plains.', or remove.

flags.sentence: ...so try things and see what works for you.
flags.suggestion: Reword: 'Note when frost or heat hits your garden and time jobs to that.' or remove.

result.overall: Most statements are clear and actionable. The weak spots are the frost answer (PKR-CGD-000027), where several lines report weather or source facts without telling the gardener what to do, and a few vague lines elsewhere. One Australia pruning-in-frost line may confuse next to the July/August advice.

result.overall: Much clearer than the first version. What remains is the frost answer, where lines still describe weather without a task, and one possible clash between pruning in July and waiting for the last frost.

after_the_second_read: Five sentences were flagged. 'Fungicide' was taken out of the New South Wales clear-up statement in version 0.3. The other four are the frost statements under 'How do I allow for frost and my own garden?': waiting for the last frost, when frosts fall, frost in valleys, and where South Australia is colder. They stay. They give no job to do; they let a gardener judge whether theirs is a frosty garden, which is what the question asks, and the pages give nothing more exact.
